title: Ā māṃ medhā: may understanding come
theme: A further verse asking Medhā, described as golden, many-formed and nourishing like a cow full of milk, to come to the speaker and favour him.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «मेधाशक्तिर्मां प्रत्या समन्तादागच्छत्विति शेषः» — may the power of medhā come to me from every side
The anonymous commentator: «सकलशास्त्रधारणक्षमत्वेन बहरूपा» — many-formed, able to hold every science
Sāyaṇa: «जगती सर्वत्र वर्तमानत्वेन जगदात्मिका» — the world itself, being present everywhere
Sāyaṇa: «जगम्या पुरुषार्थकामैर्भृशं गन्तुं योग्या» — fit to be sought eagerly by those who desire the aims of life
Sāyaṇa: «पयसा गोक्षीरादिरसेन पिन्वमानाऽस्मान्प्रीणयन्ती» — gladdening us with milk and its juices
Sāyaṇa: «सुप्रतीका सुमुखी भूत्वा» — with a gracious face
The anonymous commentator: «मां जुषतां सेवताम्» — read as singular

morphology.note: Plural in form with a singular subject (medhā); the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa gloss the singular juṣatām.
The preverb stands first with its verb unexpressed; the commentators supply ‘may she come’.

translation.literal: Hither to me [let] Medhā [come] — fragrant, of every form, golden-coloured, the world, to be sought; full of strength, swelling with milk — may she, Medhā, fair of face, favour me.
translation.readable: May Medhā come to me — fragrant, taking every form, golden, present everywhere, the goal of all who seek; strong and nourishing like a cow full of milk. May that understanding, gracious of face, favour me.

anvaya: सुरभिः विश्वरूपा हिरण्यवर्णा जगती जगम्या ऊर्जस्वती पयसा पिन्वमाना सुप्रतीका सा मेधा माम् आ [गच्छतु], माम् जुषन्ताम् ।
syntax: One verse: the preverb ā with its verb supplied and a string of epithets of medhā in the nominative, resumed by sā … medhā with the imperative juṣantām.

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator’s text reads «जहती» in the gloss where Sāyaṇa reads «जगती सर्वत्र वर्तमानत्वेन जगदात्मिका» — ‘the world, being present everywhere’; the verse’s jagatī may also name the metre, as other goddesses are hailed as metres.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: One triṣṭubh verse in two lines.

beginner: This verse continues the prayer for medhā, understanding and memory. It pictures her as a goddess: fragrant, able to take every form, golden in colour, present everywhere in the world, the goal of everyone who seeks something worth having. She is strong, and she nourishes the way a cow full of milk nourishes those who depend on her. The verse asks that this understanding, with a gracious face, come and favour the one who prays. The commentators explain her many forms as her ability to hold every branch of learning. Read together with the verses before it, it shows how highly this text values the power to learn and to keep what has been learned.
analogy: Like describing a beloved teacher by all the good things they give, before asking them to stay.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Medhā — fragrant, many-formed, golden, the world, to be sought, strong, swelling with milk, fair of face — to come to the speaker and favour him.

commentary.q: How do the commentators read the epithets?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: many-formed because she can hold every science, golden in the bodies of the deities, present everywhere as the world, to be eagerly sought by those who desire the aims of life, gladdening us with milk and its juices: «सा तथाविधगुणयुक्ता मेधा सुप्रतीका सुमुखी भूत्वा मां जुषतां सेवताम्» (Sāyaṇa).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources; the commentators read the verse as a prayer for medhā. Bhāskara’s comment on this part is missing from the edition’s copy, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse pictures understanding as food that sustains, not as a possession. Learning that keeps feeding later thought is different from facts kept for their own sake. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What idea you learned has ‘fed’ you ever since?
reflect.deeper: Why might understanding be pictured as many-formed and present everywhere?
reflect.practice: Notice one moment today when something you once learned helps you without your trying.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this verse as his anuvāka 42; the concordance maps it correctly.

flags.note: The plural juṣantām with a singular subject is read as singular with the commentators.
